I Wore the Nike Alphafly 4 Super Shoes to Run a Marathon. Here’s What I Thought.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast.
  • The Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast. That might seem an obvious observation, sure—but it applies beyond the athletes chasing finish lines to the gear they use for peak performance. So as world records fell and mass race participation swelled over the last few years, hardcore running shoe lovers wondered: Where is Nike, and what’s taking so long to unleash the brand’s next top-level super shoe?

The Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year). While the shoe has been a massively popular race day pick for all kinds of runners from 2024 on, other brands entered the super shoe space Nike originated and put out light, fast racers that offered speedier specs and took podium places (including a latest marathon world record, the first sub-2-hour finish that bested even Eliud Kipchoge’s 2019 exhibition run in an earlier Alphafly model). Nike put out some great releases in the interim, including the excellent Vomero Plus and Premium models—but the top echelon of the racing line remained untouched.

Recent findings suggest that after a nearly three-year gap, the Alphafly 4 is here. I got my feet in a pair ahead of its October 29 launch and my fall race, the NYC Marathon, so I put the super shoe to the test on the city’s streets for 26.2 miles (and a few more along the training cycle) to see if it lives up to the Alphafly name.

THE ALPHAFLY 4 builds on the same design language as its predecessor, with two of Nike’s signature Air Zoom units in the forefoot, a high stack of ZoomX foam, and a carbon fiber plate. But there are latest updates that have helped to make the shoe—at least according to Nike—lighter and more efficient.

The latest version of the Atomknit upper is a fine mesh that’s more substantial than it looks. Unlike some other top-end super shoes, Nike didn’t skimp on the outsole, with plenty of rubber coverage on the bottom. The carbon fiber plate is wider, too, and the shoe overall is roomier than previous iterations.

Still, the Alphafly 4 weighs in at about 6.6 ounces, which is on the lighter end for a mainline racing shoe (but not the lightest on the market). The foam formulation is also upcoming; the top layer is called ZoomX LT, which Nike claims is lighter and provides more energy return than the standard ZoomX, which is below the plate. That foam is stacked to 39 mm, with an 8 mm drop.

Recent findings suggest that AS I BEGAN my NYC marathon run, I could feel the Alphafly 4’s combination of plate, foam, and rocker ramping up underfoot for a fast day. The push off the pavement was effortless, and the combination of the perfect weather and unmatched vibes of the crowd made it easy to surge ahead of my target pace. But I wasn’t gunning for a PR (this was my third major race of the year, and I was more focused on maintaining a balanced pace and testing the self-serve water stations than pushing my limits).

I dialed back my excitement as I crossed the Verrazzano Bridge from the start on Staten Island, a spot that’s notorious for gassing overhyped runners leading off the race, and I was able to settle into a comfortable groove. The Alphafly 4 brought a good balance; I felt it was somewhere between the ultra-propulsive super shoes that have lately dominated the elite racing circuit and the more approachable carbon plate shoes that aren’t able to quite keep up.

Recent findings suggest that as I continued along the course, I was pleased with the consistent ride. I wasn’t exerting a ton of energy through my stride, but I was still cruising through the miles. The grippy outsole paid off as I sloshed through the water stations area, crunching crushed cups without altering my gait. I was able to just cycle my legs from step to step, allowing the rebound to push me forward.

In a recent development, when I ran the Boston Marathon earlier in the year, one of my biggest issues was the pounding my feet took on the back end of the course. I was in pain for days after, and lost my first ever toenail. As I pushed through Mile 20 and above during my NYC run, I kept expecting the pain to come. While my legs did grow heavy and my pace dropped off, my feet didn’t experience the same amount of punishment. The Alphafly 4 isn’t specifically meant for folks with wide feet by any means, but the wider base was much kinder to my tired dogs than other models I’ve worn for 26.2. I finished the race on a high note pushing for the final stretch, propelled along in part thanks to the extra push I could depend on from the shoe.

It has been revealed that THE ALPHAFLY 4 will be a reliable racer for lots of runners who want speed on the roads without going to the extremes. I appreciated the comfortable fit and smooth ride through my own race, and the propulsion provided a nice balance between less aggressive super shoes and the pace-pushing pinnacle “hyper” shoes that have started to emerge, like Puma’s Fast-R Nitro 3, Adidas’ record-breaking Pro Evo 3, and Nike’s own Apex model, which took the top spot at the NYC marathon and replaces the Alphafly line at the top of the brand’s racing stable.

Still, less experienced runners and those who expect to take four or more hours to finish a marathon might find this to be a bit too much shoe. There are other options that will both be less expensive and friendlier to slower paces. The $280 price puts the Alphafly 4 just $5 more than the comparable Adidas Adios Pro 5 (and it’s actually $5 less at launch than the Alphafly 3). Now that there are more levels of quality for super shoes, rather than just one premier shoe per brand, costs closer to $300 seem to be the norm.

In a recent development, overall, Nike has done a solid job continuing the Alphafly legacy—there are just way more super-powered racers around now than in the early days of super shoes. Still, the model is going to work for lots of runners. If you’re chasing a goal time and you need something that can be both fast and wearable, the Alphafly 4 is going to be one of your absolute top picks.

According to recent reports, brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, genesis might be a carmaker that has so far largely stuck to meat-and-potatoes models like sedans and SUVs, but the Korean luxury brand has also pumped out quite a few tantalizing concept cars in recent years. Some of them, like the G90 Wingback and Magma GT supercar, have seemed almost production-ready; others, like the X Gran Equator and X-Scorpio off-roaders, less so. But according to Automotive News, the wild X-Scorpio concept could in fact wind up in showrooms—and none other than Hyundai CEO Jose Muñoz is the one spreading the news.

“We are working with designers to try to put [the X-Scorpio] into the market,” Muñoz told AN. The feedback that Genesis received from dealers and potential customers was so positive, he mentioned, that “we are going to give it a try.”.

If the X-Scorpio does reach showrooms, it would mark yet another flank in the Hyundai Motor Group’s fast-moving and wide-ranging onslaught of off-road trucks and SUVs. Hyundai and Kia have both made clear intends for multiple body-on-frame vehicles, including ones inspired by the Hyundai Boulder concept revealed at this year’s Newly introduced York Auto Show; Genesis itself, meanwhile, has confirmed the luxurious X Gran Equator will enter production, potentially rivaling everything from the Lexus LX to the Mercedes-Benz G-wagen.

Still, none of those are anything like the X-Scorpio. In fact, there’s nothing quite like it on sale today, period. The concept, at least, is something of a cross between a Local Motors Rally Fighter and a Lamborghini Huracan Sterrato, with a twin-turbo V-8 putting out 1100 horsepower and 850 pound-feet of torque that gets sent to 40-inch off-road tires on 18-inch beadlock wheels. It was designed, the organization indicates, for the Middle East, where screaming across open terrain and sending it off sand dunes is, as the press release politely puts it, “a favorite pastime”—but considering how those are also quite popular here in the United States (see: TRX, Ram; Raptor, Ford), it seems likely a production X-Scorpio would also be a hit here.

Of course, talk is cheap, even if it’s an automotive CEO saying it. Genesis does indeed have big intends for a bunch of latest cars over the next few years, with 22 all-new or revised models coming by 2030. But whether there’s room on the balance sheet to develop for a bespoke off-road sports car with no direct competitors seems like a fairly large question mark, so let’s just keep our fingers crossed for now.

Latest Update: Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • Industry observers note that designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

Industry observers note that designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang stated in a statement.

Industry observers note that for their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

That’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

In a recent development, “We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

With their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

Next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

The research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

Industry observers note that protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

It has been revealed that the University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.

Industry News: Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • It has been revealed that tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and says it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators claims Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

It has been revealed that tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and says it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

At 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

In a recent development, FHP noted the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

It has been revealed that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

According to recent reports, it identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

Recent findings suggest that this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it indicates Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

Recent findings suggest that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Industry observers note that most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

So Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

According to recent reports, autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s key to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

Industry observers note that there’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

Industry observers note that this is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a upcoming record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

Tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

According to recent reports, we’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

It has been revealed that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

#167030. Industry News: Should You Let Your Teen Play Grand Theft Auto?

Industry News: Should You Let Your Teen Play Grand Theft Auto?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As parents, what should you and your kids consider before picking up that controller?
  • With the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, caregivers may soon find themselves negotiating with teens who insist that everyone they know is playing it.
  • “I know the difference between real life and video games.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

As parents, what should you and your kids consider before picking up that controller?

With the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, caregivers may soon find themselves negotiating with teens who insist that everyone they know is playing it.

“I know the difference between real life and video games.”.

And, of course: “Everyone else is allowed!”.

It has been revealed that yes, and everyone else may make dubious choices—not exactly a convincing argument. Grand Theft Auto is known for violence, criminal activity, sexual content, and adult themes. Surprised? It’s the sixth iteration, folks. It’s Grand Theft Auto, not Careful Driving Simulator. Yet beyond the controversy surrounding the release, there are psychological questions worth considering:.

Watching Violence Is Not the Same as Participating in It.

Kids aren’t just absorbing whatever’s on the screen. They interpret it and make their own sense of it. Video games add another wrinkle: instead of only watching a character act aggressively, players make choices and see what follows. Albert Bandura’s (2001) social cognitive theory helps us understand this. Children learn through observation, and behaviors can be rewarded or produce desirable outcomes. However, learning about a behavior is not the same as performing it. A teen who successfully steals a virtual car isn’t necessarily planning to steal the neighbor’s Honda.

Industry observers note that researchers still argue about how violent games relate to aggression. Some studies have found links with aggressive thoughts or behavior (Anderson and colleagues, 2010); others found no meaningful link between playing violent games and adolescent aggression (Przybylski and Weinstein, 2019). The answer isn’t as simple as violent game in, violent kid out. Your teenager’s brain is not one-size-fits-all. Two teens the same age can react differently to the same game. One might see the violence as exaggerated satire; another might find it upsetting or miss the point. Maturity, past experiences, and individual sensitivities matter, and age alone doesn’t tell us how a child will respond.

Recent findings suggest that age-rating systems are a helpful starting point, but the ratings don’t explain how parents can understand developmental differences. Adults can consider a child’s maturity, awareness of specific content, and ability to distinguish fictional scenarios from real-world behavior. Understanding that something is fictional doesn’t mean a child is emotionally prepared for it.

For teens, video games aren’t necessarily just games. They’re opportunities for social connection, common experiences, and participation in peer culture. Belonging is especially important during adolescence. Being excluded from something friends are discussing or playing can feel like being excluded from the group itself.

In a recent development, that doesn’t mean parents should say yes to help their child fit in. But a teen’s interest in the fresh Grand Theft Auto may be less about virtual crime than about joining a conversation their friends are having. Ask what appeals to them: the story, exploring the world, the humor, or that everyone’s talking about it? Hear them out. This may be better than shutting the conversation down with an automatic no. What does the game teach? Rather than focusing on the violence, consider: What aggressive behavior is rewarded, how are consequences portrayed, how is satire used to criticize society, and would younger players take it literally?

Talk it through with your kids. They’re still learning how to make sense of complicated stories, relationships, and questions about right and wrong. And humor adds a further layer. Grand Theft Auto is known for exaggerated social commentary and dark humor. Still, understanding satire requires distinguishing between what is depicted and what is being criticized.

A younger player may recognize that a character is behaving badly without understanding the larger social commentary. Even when adolescents recognize satire, that doesn’t automatically mean every aspect of the content is appropriate for them.

Before spending money on the latest installment of virtual criminal behavior, parents might want to do a little research:.

Conversations about how the game portrays violence, relationships, and consequences can help kids think critically about what they’re seeing.

It has been revealed that parental controls can manage access, purchases, and playtime. Remember, restricting a game at home doesn’t necessarily prevent children from encountering it through friends, YouTube, or social media. We were once kids too. Don’t tell me that while reading this, you didn't remember something you did outside your home that your parents still don’t know about.

Is Grand Theft Auto VI Worth It?

Adults who enjoy open-world narratives may believe it is worth it. When a 12-year-old indicates everyone already has it, we might have to reconsider. Recognize how gaming matters to your teen without buying the game. Their interest deserves a conversation; your boundaries continue to matter. We don’t need another moral panic about video games. However, we also don’t need to pretend that all media experiences are appropriate for every child. Sometimes the most responsible parenting decision is to say yes. Sometimes it’s to say no. And sometimes it’s to say, “Let’s find out a little more about this game before I spend my hard-earned money on your virtual crime spree.”.

After all, just because a game allows you to steal a car doesn’t mean parents should abandon the driver’s seat.

Violent video game effects on aggression, empathy, and prosocial behavior in Eastern and Western countries: A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 136(2), 151–173. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018251.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

It has been revealed that the game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

According to recent reports, the latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Industry observers note that battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

Industry observers note that november’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

It has been revealed that given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

Latest Update: Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.
  • Industry observers note that the risk for cancer became higher as weight increased.
  • This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

Industry observers note that the risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

It has been revealed that body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:.

In a recent development, over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:.

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all newly introduced cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

It has been revealed that previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study highlighted a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who right now smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he stated.

The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America.
  • Most people today haven’t heard of it.
  • That loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America. The wooden steamship helped connect San Francisco with Upcoming York City before the construction of a coast-to-coast rail network, and sank off the coast of South Carolina in 1857.

425 people died. Most people today haven’t heard of it.

That loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship. But the SS Central America was also hauling $1.2 million worth of gold, according to a 1992 court case about the wreck. Given the current value of gold, that’s around $236 million in today’s dollars. And that’s just what’s documented: the ship had a number of wealthy passengers, who were likely carrying their own gold, so the total could be even higher.

In a recent development, A ship full of gold, sunk and lost for over a century. It’s odd that the ship isn’t a household name. And the story keeps getting weirder: the wreck contributed to a massive recession, and when treasure hunters found the ship in the 1980s, decades of lawsuits followed.

Say you wanted to get from San Francisco to New York City in the 1850s. Going over land was miserable—cars were a half century away, and there weren’t many roads. There wasn’t even a rail line connecting the two coasts. Your best bet was to take a ship down to what is now Panama, a train across that narrow bit of land, and then another ship up to New York.

Industry observers note that the SS Central America served the Atlantic part of that journey. It left the east coast of Panama on September 3, 1857, with 592 people on board. The ship had one other stop: Havana, Cuba. By September 8, when the ship was leaving that port, the weather looked great, according to a writeup by the US Naval Institute.

It has been revealed that that changed—hurricane-force winds battered the wooden hull. By September 11, the crew was working to bail out the ship, and by noon every man joined them. It wasn’t enough: by 2pm the water reached the boilers, leaving the ship drifting. The bailing continued all night, and for a while it seemed like the weather would clear up long enough for a full evacuation. It wasn’t to be—the storm resumed by mid-morning. The captain signaled a nearby ship, the Marine, for help. Only 100 people—including the 59 women and children—boarded the Marine.

It has been revealed that the captain went down with the ship around 8pm local time, along with most of the remaining men, who were pulled in by the undertow of the sinking ship. The few men who survived did so by grabbing doors, chairs, and anything else still floating, until another ship—the Ellen—could find them. In total, 425 people lost their lives.

Industry observers note that the human cost was high, but there was also a huge economic fallout. A 1992 paper by Lawrence D. Stone, the researcher whose work led to the rediscovery of the wreck, states that the gold on board was intended to shore up several banks already on the brink of collapse. Within a month, almost all banks in the US stopped offering gold in exchange for paper money.

Sources indicate that naturally, a ship this famous—with this much gold on board—became a bit of a legend. Countless people attempted to find the wreck, but no one succeeded until the Columbus-America Discovery Group of Ohio found the wreck in the 1980s. The crew was led by treasure hunter Tommy Gregory Thompson.

The discovery happened thanks to advanced technology—sonar and state-of-the-art remote-controlled submarines. But also because of math.

Sources indicate that stone, whose work I mentioned earlier, explained his method in a 1992 paper. He employed Bayesian search theory. This method begins with finding hypotheses about where the wreck may be, judging how likely each theory is, and ultimately making a map outlining the probability of the ship being in various areas. A route for the search is designed to start with the highest probability areas, continuing from there to lower probabilities.

It has been revealed that the survey took 40 days, covering 1,400 square miles of ocean off the Carolina coast. The wreck ended up being in a relatively low probability area, though one included in the route. In 1988, a remotely operated vehicle provided a view of the wreck.

“The storybook result would have been for the Central America to have been found in a high probability area near the beginning of the search,” wrote Stone. “Given the actual result, what can we say about the value of the procedures for developing the search initiative? The most obvious thing to say is that they worked.”.

That’s the thing about probability: the most likely thing isn’t always what’s true. That doesn’t mean it’s not worth calculating—it can still lead to good results.

But what about the gold? Over the next few years the team brought up most of the commercial gold shipment. A federal judge put its bullion value at about $21 million in 1993, but coins and ingots from a famous shipwreck are worth far more to collectors. In 2000, the bulk of it sold for about $50 million. Today most of the gold is in the hands of private collectors.

Recent findings suggest that this would normally be where the story ends: the treasure is found, the treasure hunters get paid, and everyone is happy. That’s not what happened this time.

By 1989, the insurance companies that covered the SS Central America back in the 1850s argued that the gold belonged to them. Their logic: We paid damages to clients who lost the gold, therefore it’s ours. The insurance companies lost that lawsuit, but it was only the beginning.

Thompson took $12.5 million from investors to fund the treasure hunt. Those investors sued in 2005, alleging they never got any proceeds from the treasure, even after the 2000 sale of the gold. Several members of Thompson’s crew sued in 2006. Thompson went into hiding in 2012, only to be arrested in 2015. He wasn’t released until March of 2026. Some 500 gold coins remain unaccounted for.

It’s an odd footnote to a fascinating story of history, math, and science. And who knows? Maybe this story will still be going a hundred years in the future.

And there may be more to the story of the SS Central America. A 2018 expedition recovered more gold from a safe on the ship, in a passenger compartment. There could be more down there.

Is Yeti’s Latest Performance Outdoor Clothing Any Good? I Put It to the Test to Find Out.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • Sources indicate that IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently launched a performance outdoor clothing line.
  • We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently launched a performance outdoor clothing line. It’s a deviation, sure, but perhaps a sensible one given the brand’s commitment to outdoor gear and all things insulation. As frequent testers of upcoming products in this ever-expanding category, we could not resist the chance to throw them on and put them through the paces in the elements.

We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip. For context, the other two pieces are the Caprock Merino Quarter-Zip and the Heuco 310 Full-Zip, essentially siblings of the fleece we tried out. To the brand’s credit, no PFAs are used in the line and all items come with a three-year warranty.

Before even testing, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. The pieces show some clear restraint from a brand that tends toward boldness and large logos (you know, like the beloved coolers). You’d barely even know these were Yeti tops, as you really have to hunt for the brand stamp. And there’s a less-is-more approach in the design here, clearly made with active lifestyles and packability in mind (even color-wise, there are only two options max per item, a somewhat refreshing factoid).

Recent findings suggest that I tried all three pieces over a couple of weeks in the dead of fall in the Pacific Northwest. Translation? They were subjected to downpours, foggy night jogs, chilly mornings, and windy afternoons. I wore them on long walks with the dog, bike commutes in the rain, adventures on muddy trails, and to evening soccer games. I even brought them to the coast during a storm that stirred up high surf and sideways precipitation. Here’s what I think after all the initial testing.

The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket looks good, there’s no denying as much. The sleek, trim fit works for even the most active functions and we found it never overheated in testing. Lightweight and packable, it’s somewhat nimble thanks to two-way stretch fabric but not as much so as the other two items tested.

It has been revealed that the water resistance is also impressive. I walked the dog through a downpour in this jacket for about 30 minutes and came back with just a few moisture spots on my layer beneath. Not bad for a jacket that certainly doesn’t claim to be waterproof (though does sport a water-repellant finish). In drizzle and light rain, you’re just fine in this puffer jacket. In fact, the water would bead up with the same intensity even after many wears, meaning that exterior was done right.

Recent findings suggest that while I liked the felt-lined pockets, I think they could be even warmer. The blend of Expedry Down and traceable European Lavalan Wool insulation is perhaps the jacket’s strongest feature. Going with a hybrid blend affords an ability to tightrope walk that fine-line between breathability and protection from the elements—and the proof was in the performance.

At $400 though, this is not a cheap item by any stretch of the imagination.

According to recent reports, this was my favorite piece of the trio, and arguably the most straightforward. From the superior YKK Aquaguard zipper to the extremely packable nature of the jacket, the Tilloo is a genuine winner. Like a substantial boss in your favorite video game, so many jackets in the category have a weak spot hidden somewhere. It usually translates to water seeping in from a cuff or finding its way in through an average zipper. Not here—this jacket is watertight yet breathable.

One of the coolest features is just how quiet this jacket is. As somebody born and raised in the Pacific Northwest, I’ve worn a fair number of waterproof shells. Many of them swish loudly as you move (not unlike Jim Carrey in Dumb and Dumber as he’s pretending to run while driving). This less crinkly option is quite quiet, a bonus you perhaps never knew you desired (but once you have it, it’s hard to go back).

Industry observers note that if you’re like me, you like to get outdoors to get away from all the noise. A loud jacket can disrupt an adventure, whether you’re birding in a marsh or scanning for wildlife on a hike. This jacket is not silent but it’s noticeably more hushed than most others, even during animated motions and heavy exercise. The Velcro cuffs create nice clasps over base layers (or just above a smartwatch during a run) while the liner itself is fairly soft to the touch, unlike the less appealing, membrane-like feel you get from so many options. The hood is adjustable and offers a nice panorama without hampering much of your view. And the way it pulls rain off is impressive, meaning you never have to shake off pooling areas like you might with a lesser jacket or umbrella.

It has become my go-to for offseason excursions. While $350 is an undeniable expense, the jacket is worth the price.

Straight on, the Sansaba Fleece 260 is incredibly soft (like, you’re gonna want to nuzzle it). The proprietary PrimaLoft Bio Fleece is a sensory joy, with a lovely feel and a density level that seems to hit the Goldilocks spot. Best, it’s a composite of 100% post-consumer recycled materials. These shorter fibers are densely distributed, creating what Yeti classifies as a midweight garment. We’d argue that it performs on the higher end of the spectrum, at least in terms of insulation and warmth. No, it wouldn’t quite cut it on its own for significant stretches in below-freezing conditions, but it does just find in the kind of cold we’re normally subjected to.

Industry observers note that the fleece also breathes quite well. I found that it paired nicely with a brisk mountain hike or even a sweaty workout in damp conditions. However, playing under anything more than a light drizzle requires a proper shell to fend off precipitation. We liked the length of the collar, stylish yet still significant enough to hide under during chilly gusts of wind.

Billed as a fleece made for movement and strenuous activities, the Sansaba fared pretty well. I really put it to the sword one day, zipping it up for a four-mile run in light rain. Normally, I’d wear a long-sleeve moisture-wicking shirt beneath, but I wanted to see how the fleece would fare atop a regular cotton T-shirt. While it did well at fending off light moisture and pulling some of the sweat from my arms, I was pretty soaked in sweat at the end. A pretty easy fix with a better undershirt, sure, but it indicates that perhaps the fleece can’t quite do the most strenuous activities without an unwanted side effect (props for drying so promptly after the fact, however).

Additional cons? The interior of the pockets could use some work. The plain mesh is boring and doesn’t do much to warm the paws. But the fleece is so warm and welcoming throughout the top that you can just rest your hands elsewhere for a quick warm-up. The collar also hugs the neck nicely. This is bittersweet, as it really cradles the area and keeps it warm; however, if you like to duck your chin and mouth (and a little nose) beneath this part of a top during a wind gust, it’s harder to do as it’s fairly snug. For $180, this is a pretty good deal, but not necessarily superior to several other fleeces at a similar price point.

According to recent reports, while you don’t need the whole set, you might want a few of these pieces to bolster your outdoor apparel game. I recommend them all, but with some caveats. The rain jacket is the best item for the price and is very much on par with others in the category.

The puffer is nice but I don’t find it a whole lot better than, say, this one from Wren that I’ve been wearing for a couple of years now (the Columbia Terwilliger Treail Heat Seal Jacket is another fine option). The neat, textured, and non-glossy (per so, so many) look is hard to beat, but it’s a significant chunk of change even give its merits.

The fleece is also an attractive piece of outerwear with some high-performance capabilities, but perhaps not at the same level as some of its counterparts at its decidedly high price point. I tends toward options like the Patagonia Better Jacket and the Trailmade from REI, a bargain-and-a-half. But the Sansaba is an undoubtedly good-looking option with a lot going for it.

Yeti is clearly on to something here and has turned heads with a combination of clean fits, useful tech, and designs with mobility in mind (not to mention some environmentally conscious moves too). But this writer would suggest splurging on perhaps just one of the items depending on your adventuring angles and lifestyle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Hyundai Elantra continues to defy the apparent incipient death of the sedan, and the Korean automaker just gave it a major upgrade for 2027. Between a new “Art of Steel” design, a larger size, and upgraded infotainment technology, the 2027 Hyundai Elantra is more prepared for the future than ever before.

According to recent reports, revealed Thursday at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show, the 2027 Elantra's most obvious feature is its exterior design. Created under Hyundai's new Art of Steel design philosophy, which was first revealed on the Boulder concept, the Elantra is now a boxy beast with wide fenders, sharp headlights, and a square rear end. This new sedan was designed with a very clear three-box configuration and sport sedan dynamism in mind, according to Hyundai’s head of design.

“There is an inherent beauty in a sedan because its proportions are honest, intuitive and functional,” stated SangYup Lee, executive vice president and head of the Hyundai and Genesis Global Design Center. “With the all-latest Elantra, we returned to that essence, then pushed it forward. Wide, muscular fenders, a long hood, and refined three-box proportions give Elantra a confident, athletic presence that challenges the conventions of the compact sedan.”.

In addition to the latest exterior design, changes under the skin mean the latest Elantra is now 3.3 inches longer, 1.1 inches wider, and features a 1.1-inch longer wheelbase than its predecessor; all told, Hyundai claims the 2027 Elantra has over one inch more rear headroom and legroom. So-called H-Edge lighting, futuristic grille styling, slim- neck mirrors, and lift-up flush door handles make up the rest of the visual changes.

But Hyundai didn’t stop its design renovations with the exterior. Inside the Elantra, the carmaker added a newly introduced Curve of Upholstery design and an asymmetrical front layout, which is meant to “gently embrace” the driver. A central 12.9-inch Pleos Connect infotainment system is standard on all Elantra models, while an available slim information display in the driver’s natural line of sight provides critical driving information. Other interior features include 15-kW dual wireless phone charging, Audio by Bang & Olufsen, Hyundai Digital Key 2, and 100-watt ultra-fast charging USB ports. Upholstery will be available in four black color combinations, as well as Burgundy/Rose Ivory and Chalk Beige.

Sources indicate that mechanically, the Elantra is a bit less exciting. The fresh model will offer two powertrain options: a 1.6-liter hybrid four-cylinder powerplant, and a naturally-aspirated 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine. The hybrid model will deliver 154 horsepower through a six-speed dual-clutch transmission, while the purely internal combustion model offers 146 horsepower routed through a continuously variable transmission. Hybridized Elantra models also feature a predictive drive system that intelligently anticipates driving patterns and road conditions to maximize efficiency, as well as a new “Stay Mode” that lets the climate control, stereo, charging ports and other non-motion-related functions operate for up to 30 minutes with the engine off.

It has been revealed that the pure ICE version will arrive as a 2027 model year Elantra, while the newly introduced Hyundai Elantra Hybrid will debut as a 2028 model year vehicle. Specific on-sale timing, pricing, fuel economy ratings and other details will be revealed closer to the vehicle’s American launch.

The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#167023. How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (834 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite.
  • Recent findings suggest that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk.
  • A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

Recent findings suggest that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

In a recent development, early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, indicates Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”.

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

Other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

According to recent reports, images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

According to recent reports, the moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

According to recent reports, but some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley notes samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” notes Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

What would happen if Yellowstone’s ‘supervolcano’ erupted today?

Recent findings suggest that is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Ahead of prepares by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

In a recent development, “You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” states Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) blueprint to adopt this reusable design.

Industry observers note that even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley claims the ESA has made looks to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into latest materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley says that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” says Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”.

According to recent reports, that lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

#167022. Industry News: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1741 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • But that simple statement also hides something crucial.
  • Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something crucial. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a new generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

It has been revealed that alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

It has been revealed that that’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

According to recent reports, someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

According to recent reports, for years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

This isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

In a recent development, battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

For decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly promptly into larger machines. Often though, newly introduced riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely fresh generation on electric two-wheelers.

Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

It has been revealed that there’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

The rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

It has been revealed that they’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

Sources indicate that and electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

My argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more notable, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

In a recent development, what excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:.

Recent findings suggest that I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

Recent findings suggest that I never rode impaired. That was easy.

Recent findings suggest that I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

After a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

It has been revealed that I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

None of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a newly introduced category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG. Black Budget has been sort of floating around the internet for months, but Krafton never really committed to revealing core details about the game, or when players will actually get to play it.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Sources indicate that black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

Coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios says the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

In a recent development, the game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

Industry observers note that as it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

Though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

9 rescued orangutans returned to the wild in Indonesia

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires.
  • Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires.
  • Sources indicate that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

Sources indicate that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially crucial, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

Experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

“We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” noted Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”.

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.
