Industry News: Plant-Based Milk Alternatives May Not Give You Enough Iodine. Here’s Why That Matters

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.
  • According to recent reports, the United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine.
  • In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

According to recent reports, the United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine. This compares with 61% for calcium and 46% for vitamin B12.

In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.

The study found that replacing as little as 20% of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives could increase the risk of inadequate iodine intake, particularly among adolescent girls and women of reproductive age.

Recent findings suggest that “People often worry about a decline in calcium intake when they replace some of their dairy with plant-based alternatives. As a result, iodine is frequently overlooked. This study serves as a valuable reminder of iodine’s significance as a nutrient,” noted Victoria Finn, MD, board certified endocrinologist at Medical Offices of Manhattan, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included analysis of UK plant-based milk, cheese, and yogurt products, as well as dietary data from 3,500 people.

The researchers used statistical modeling to predict how swapping dairy for PBAs might affect iodine and other nutrients.

The people who are most vulnerable to iodine inadequacy are adolescent females and people at reproductive age, especially those who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant.

The researchers estimated that replacing 20% to 35% of dairy intake with PBAs would increase the proportion of people with inadequate iodine intake:.

Sources indicate that when the researchers modeled the replacement of all dairy products with PBAs, the proportion of adolescent females with inadequate iodine intake rose to 80%. Among females ages 19 to 49, that proportion remained relatively stable as replacement rates increased.

It is vital to keep in mind that the study used dietary modeling rather than direct measurement of iodine status.

Iodine is crucial for thyroid hormone production, metabolism, and both fetal and child brain development.

“Your thyroid gland requires iodine to produce thyroid hormones, which play a crucial role in regulating metabolism and supporting normal growth and development,” mentioned Finn.

According to recent reports, she added that if you consistently consume too little iodine over an extended period, the thyroid gland may enlarge and eventually struggle to produce enough hormones. This condition is known as hypothyroidism, which can lead to various symptoms such as lethargy, sleepiness, weight gain, dry skin, and more.

“Hypothyroidism can be particularly dangerous during pregnancy, as the baby’s brain, nervous system, and organs rely heavily on the mother’s thyroid hormone during the early stages of development,” Finn added.

In the United Kingdom, dairy is a major iodine source due to cattle feed supplementation, not because dairy is naturally high in iodine.

In the United States, dairy is also an important source of iodine for the same reasons.

However, the risk profile for iodine deficiency in the U.S. may differ from the U.K., as iodized salt is also a significant source of iodine and is widely available in the U.S., but not in the U.K.

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the recommended daily intake of iodine depends on your age.

Plant-based or plant-forward diets have grown in popularity, in part due to the health benefits they offer. For example, consuming less meat can reduce your risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol.

Recent findings suggest that however, as this study suggests, it may be possible to reduce your iodine intake when transitioning to a plant-based diet. There are ways you can protect your iodine intake when choosing a more plant-forward diet, though.

According to recent reports, check the labels on plant-based dairy alternatives to find those fortified with iodine. You can also read the nutrition label. Iodine may be listed as potassium iodide or potassium iodate.

Seafood, eggs, and iodized salt are all good sources of iodine.

You can also discuss iodine supplements with your healthcare professional.

According to recent reports, “Iodine supplements should be taken with caution, especially without checking your thyroid levels,” remarked Finn. “Additionally, be cautious with kelp supplements, as their iodine content can vary, and excessive iodine intake can disrupt thyroid function.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials strategy to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

According to recent reports, the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Industry observers note that korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with latest tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

The sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han says he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student stated in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place fresh anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin swiftly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Sources indicate that concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

According to recent reports, while fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be new concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Sources indicate that creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

#166936. Breaking: Never Before in the History of Motoring: How the Splendor and Madness Of the Aughts Shaped Today’s Car World

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1345 w)

Breaking: Never Before in the History of Motoring: How the Splendor and Madness Of the Aughts Shaped Today’s Car World

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the driver’s seat of a 2005 Ford GT, with my best pal riding shotgun, I stared through the windshield with eyes opened as wide as the car’s headlights.
  • This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.
  • It felt like driving a Michigan-made Millennium Falcon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was a perfect moment. In the driver’s seat of a 2005 Ford GT, with my best pal riding shotgun, I stared through the windshield with eyes opened as wide as the car’s headlights. The year was 2007. We were on a stretch of I-80 that dives down the eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada mountains, from California into Nevada. The early-­morning sun hung low on the horizon in front of us. Looking out on the desert, we saw miles of empty highway, with visibility so sharp that we would see any highway patrol vehicle in our path.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

It felt like driving a Michigan-made Millennium Falcon. This Ford could hit 200 mph and beat the Ferrari Challenge Stradale around a road course. It was shamelessly retro, trading hard on the Le Mans pedigree of its GT40 ancestor, but it was also new age and American as all hell. It felt unprecedented.

Looking back now, almost 20 years later, I can see that the word unprecedented applied to the whole decade. The Aughts, defined as the years 2000 to 2009, were packed with never-before events and spectacular vehicles such as the Ford GT. It was a time of excitement and optimism, when cars were cool and quicker than ever—until it all crashed into a ditch with the economic downturn. The era was to the car industry what the Sixties were to music, politics, and assassinations. An era of profound change. Of tremendous upheaval. Of darkness and light. Of death and rebirth.

It was the decade that shaped our here and now.

On the most macro level, the Aughts were when the global automotive ecosphere began ­reordering itself into what we know today. In 2008, ­Toyota overtook GM to become the world’s largest automaker, selling 8.97 million vehicles around the world that year. The ­DaimlerChrysler partner­ship shattered. General Motors, one of the largest corporations on earth, and Chrysler, another of Detroit’s Major Three, went bankrupt at the end of the decade, and if not for the federal government handing out bags of cash to bail out those legendary companies, they might no longer exist.

GM’s Oldsmobile and Pontiac, two brands that collectively had made cars for nearly 200 years, disappeared during the Aughts. (To be fair, Pontiac did make it a few days into the newly introduced decade, ending production on January 4, 2010, with a last-gasp G6 sedan.) Plymouth also went bye-bye. Saturn assembled its final vehicle in 2009.

The Aughts were also the start of credible alternatives to internal-combustion motoring’s hegemony. The Toyota Prius arrived in the United States in July 2000, then became a cultural lightning rod when sales of the second-­generation model exploded in response to surging gas prices. Hybrid, a term that often applied to a kind of cannabis at the time, suddenly became lingo referring to a kind of car. At the same time, there were inklings of a lithium-ion automotive future. Tesla put out its first battery-powered car, the Roadster, in 2008, and early adopters felt the shock of a 0–60 thrust without the jolt of gears changing. Cars began to morph from machinery into the rolling computer devices that we drive today, as screens proliferated on dashboards and our phones learned to talk to our vehicles. Digital technology wormed its way deeper into every aspect of motoring, a trend that continues, albeit with far less idealism now.

The decade was a history-defining time in motorsport as well. Globally, racing saw the dawn of a upcoming dynastic epoch. Michael Schumacher, driving for Ferrari, claimed the Formula 1 world championship from 2000 to 2005. In large part, F1 has been a series defined by dynasties ever since. Audi and Tom Kristensen ruled Le Mans for nearly the entire decade, and for the first time, a turbo­diesel won: the R10 in 2006. In NASCAR, Jimmie Johnson took the Cup Series title five years in a row with Chevrolet starting in 2006.

Industry observers note that dynasties on this level of dominance had never happened before in any of these series. I remember sitting in a press conference after the Italian Grand Prix in 2006, when Schumacher (having just won the race) revealed his first retirement. The moment he unleashed the news, he teared up and an explosion of camera flashes came from the press corps. The feeling in the room was unforgettable. What Schumacher had done during his career to that point was unprecedented.

Even pop culture had an auto­motive renaissance. The Fast and the Furious premiered on June 18, 2001, with three sequels in multiplexes before the decade was over. F&F grew into Universal Studios’ biggest film franchise and remains the most successful car-movie series ever. Pixar’s Cars came out in 2006 and became Paul Newman’s highest-grossing film, even though viewers never saw his face. Talladega Nights (also 2006) may not invite many critical superlatives, but it unapologetically roasted NASCAR, which was in on the joke. It also popularized the saying, “If you ain’t first, you’re last.” Michael Bay’s Transformers films filled theaters. There was even a Dukes of Hazzard movie with Jessica Simpson playing Daisy Duke, Burt Reynolds as Boss Hogg, and a badass General Lee Dodge Charger. Car video games saw surging popularity, sales, and advancements in graphics. The Aughts gave us Forza Motorsport, plus latest and series-defining installments of Gran Turismo and Grand Theft Auto.

Sources indicate that so much was happening in the car world that being a fan felt electrifying. The Camaro, the Charger, and the Challenger were back, and the Mustang was reborn in retro style. The first Cars & Coffee events happened in Southern California, and soon small towns around the U.S. were hosting them.

When you throw all of this together, it made for an earth-shattering decade. Despite the dizzying news cycle, however, it was the cars themselves that we remember most. The Aughts ushered in a new era for halo cars, when automakers set out to build masterpieces that created new expectations for performance and technology. Some would say the Seventies, Eighties, and Nineties were halcyon days for car fans. But the new sheetmetal that graced our roads in the first decade of the new millennium was incomparable.

Ford came up with the aforementioned GT, which was the first real Ford customer supercar made in any significant numbers. Porsche gave us the Carrera GT, a mid-engine rocket ship that is one of the greatest sports cars of all time. Bugatti chased even bigger numbers with the Veyron, the first road car that could crack 250 mph and produce 1000 hp.

According to recent reports, there were plenty of other highlights as soaring corporate confidence and unheard-of development budgets ushered in the arrival of still more icons. This was the decade of the C6 Corvette Z06 and ZR1, the Audi R8, the Ferrari Enzo, and the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren. The Bentley Continental GT and the Porsche 911 GT3 RS debuted, along with the U.S.-eligible Nissan GT-R. V-8 engines were squeezed into the BMW M3, the Cadillac CTS-V, and the Mercedes-Benz C63 AMG. It was a time of heroes.

Recent findings suggest that these cars didn’t just thrill us; they were so unique and outstanding that they redefined the identities of the brands that made them and even motoring itself. That is the true legacy of the Aughts. Even if you’re too young to have lived through those years, you are reaping the rewards today. Because of all of that innovation and ambition, the future through our windshields still looks bright. But maybe a little less bright than it did back then.

A.J. Baime is the author of seven books, including Go Like Hell: Ford, Ferrari, and Their Battle for Speed and Glory at Le Mans, and The Accidental President: Harry S. Truman and the Four Months that Changed the World. An R&T editor-at-large, he has driven cars on racetracks all over the U.S. and Europe, going back to 2007. He is proudly the R&T staff’s slowest track driver.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the time has arrived for another Arc Raiders enhancement, and Embark has certainly delivered. Today’s patch, version 1.6.0, is among the smallest the game has received so far, focusing almost exclusively on disabling map exploits.

Perhaps more key than the patch itself, however, is the announcement the developer made around it.

It has been revealed that starting off with patch 1.6.0, it takes out a particular zipline on Stella Montis, the game’s most recent addition ot the map roster. Some players used said zipline to get out of bounds, something the game has been battling on several of its maps.

According to recent reports, on Blue Gate, the patch fixes a collision problem that allowed players to vault through a wall, and fall to their death. The map fixes continue with another on Spaceport Launch Tower, which takes out a gap in collision that players have been able to shoot through.

According to recent reports, the last change in this upgrade affects gameplay feel around Arc enemies. Certain materials in the game’s world weren’t blocking their vision - or fire - when they should have, and this has now been fixed.

Recent findings suggest that alongside today’s patch, Embark also unveiled that going forward, we’re going to see fewer patches for Arc Raiders. The game has been getting updates almost every Thursday since it debuted in late October.

Now that most of the major problems have been fixed, the studio is shifting to a slower patching cadence. Critical fixes will still be issued as soon as they’re developed, but don’t expect a patch each week going forward.

Recent findings suggest that embark also revealed that patch releases and in-game store rotations will now occur on Tuesdays. You should also expect the next few weeks to be quiet, as members of the team go on holiday breaks.

Sources indicate that but, before everyone goes away, the game is going to get one more major enhancement. The last item on Arc Raiders’ roadmap, revealed in early November, is the Cold Snap event. This is on track for Tuesday, bringing some new content alongside a few other fixes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

According to recent reports, last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

“Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo stated in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”.

The zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”.

Industry observers note that on Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a fresh approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, residents of Fresh Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief. A dangerous menace to society has been taken off the streets after police apprehended a 75-year-old man accused of leading deputies on a high-stakes electric bike chase at speeds reaching a blistering 16 mph (26 km/h).

According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.

What followed was apparently the world’s slowest police chase.

Mitchell reportedly continued riding along the beach, eventually exiting onto city streets, where he allegedly rode against traffic before making it back to his home. Deputies followed him, and when Mitchell attempted to retreat into his garage, he reportedly resisted arrest by grabbing onto a golf cart and refusing to let go.

The ordeal ended with Mitchell in custody, facing four charges, including felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area. His bond was set at $4,000.

And just like that, another dangerous electric bicycle criminal was brought to justice. This was clearly a success story like no other, and American streets are now safer.

Recent findings suggest that now, before anyone gets too worked up, let’s be clear: I’m not suggesting that e-bike riders should be allowed to ignore traffic laws, endanger pedestrians, or flee from police. Reports indicate that Mitchell was riding recklessly around beachgoers, including children, and that’s certainly something worth addressing. And once he allegedly decided to flee from deputies, he turned what could have been a minor infraction into a much more serious situation.

But can we also acknowledge how absurd this whole thing is?

We’ve reached a point where a 75-year-old man riding a bicycle at 16 mph can end up the subject of a police pursuit and felony charges, while we’ve largely accepted that multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and seriously injure people on our roads as an unavoidable cost of modern transportation.

It has been revealed that every day, drivers speed through neighborhoods, roll through stop signs, stare at their phones, and operate vehicles capable of killing pedestrians with a moment’s inattention. Or perhaps I shouldn’t say ‘capable’, but rather that they do. 40,000 people every year die in the US from car violence. Yet somehow, electric bicycles have become one of the great transportation menaces of our time, despite contributing much, much less to major bodily harm or death.

It has been revealed that and yes, there are absolutely legitimate concerns about dangerous riding. I’ve repeatedly argued that we need better enforcement, especially when it comes to teenagers riding high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths. Those aren’t electric bicycles, and treating them as such has created a real problem for everyone.

But if we’re going to devote police resources to cracking down on dangerous two-wheeled behavior, perhaps we could start there instead of turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century.

What is absurd is that he didn't simply stop and follow the officer's directions to slow down. If he is going to try to flee from the police by riding dangerously including going against traffic then he should face charges. As presumably a first time offender, he'll be given probation if he agrees not to do it again.

To be fair, Mitchell’s alleged behavior after being stopped certainly didn’t help his case. But the larger point remains: our priorities around road safety have become wildly distorted.

We’ve normalized the dangers of cars so thoroughly that we barely blink at the daily carnage they cause, yet we’re increasingly treating comparatively low-speed electric bicycles as an existential threat to public safety.

Recent findings suggest that I’m all for enforcing sensible e-bike rules. I’m all for throwing the book at major infractions and scofflaws who pose a public menace. But I’m also for applying a little perspective.

Industry observers note that because if a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph is among our most pressing transportation safety concerns, then I have some very good news about the state of our roads. But unfortunately, there is no good news to share today.

Infant Bleeding Cases Surge as More Parents Refuse Vitamin K Shots for Newborns

  • A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.
  • A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two large studies published on November 5 link declining newborn vitamin K shot rates to a sharp increase in infant bleeding cases, including potentially fatal brain hemorrhages.

A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.

A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S. infants, found that refusal rates more than doubled, rising from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who did not receive the shot had a 47% higher risk of bleeding and more than twice the risk of intracranial bleeding.

Additionally, newly introduced data from Truveta suggest the trend is continuing: refusals of vitamin K shots increased by 57% between January and June 2026, rising from 5.2% to 8.1% of newborns.

Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and newborns naturally have very low levels. Without the preventive injection, infants are at risk for VKDB, which can cause sudden bleeding in the brain, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs. Late-onset VKDB can occur up to six months after birth, often without warning signs, and may be fatal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) continue to recommend an intramuscular vitamin K injection for all newborns, ideally within 6 hours of birth.

Sources indicate that the shot is not a vaccine; it is a nutrient injection that helps prevent dangerous bleeding. A single dose reduces the risk of late-onset VKDB by approximately 98%.

Experts not involved in the studies attribute the rise in refusals partly to broader vaccine hesitancy and mixed public health messaging.

“The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision,” noted Graham Tse, MD, a pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

Recent findings suggest that some of these factors, Tse said, include conflicting messages from federal health agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), both overseen by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., an outspoken critic of the childhood immunization schedule.

Sources indicate that the vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, yet RFK Jr. has declined to reassure parents about its safety, despite the CDC’s current recommendation to administer it at birth.

Additionally, growing medical distrust among parents has led to refusal of routine newborn care, such as the vitamin K shot, Reuters reports.

Healthline spoke with Tse to learn more about the risks of refusing the vitamin K shot and what new or expectant parents should know about this routine newborn treatment.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Tse: The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision.

A contributing factor to the decline in vitamin K injection at birth, as well as in newborn hepatitis B vaccination, is the conflicting messages from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Recommendations from these entities and others are conflicting or do not align with established, research-based, and proven recommendations from organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

When there are conflicting recommendations, it creates confusion and doubt among parents about what the best or right choice is for their child.

As well, there is so much misinformation on the internet, among influencers, and on social media that it is difficult to know what information is accurate, well-researched, and proven, versus what may be just someone’s opinion or belief.

In a recent development, some are mistaking the vitamin K injection at birth for a vaccination, which it is not. Ultimately, all these factors are contributing to parents declining or delaying vitamin K injections at birth.

It has been revealed that tse: Declining the newborn vitamin K injection puts the newborn at significant risk of serious and life threatening complications from vitamin K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). This was previously referred to as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

VKDB can be as mild as bruising of the skin but can be as serious as bleeding into the brain, and newborns and infants can die from VKDB.

Declining vitamin K injection at birth is significant because of the serious and potentially life threatening consequences of deficiency of Vitamin K and not being able to clot the blood.

The vitamin K injection at birth is highly effective at preventing VKDB.

Tse: If a neonate or infant has vitamin K deficiency, the ability to clot their blood and stop bleeding is highly reduced.

All newborns are at risk of low vitamin K due to low body stores, low vitamin K content of breast milk, reduced ability of the gut to mobilize vitamin K, and poor transfer of vitamin K across the placenta.

In a recent development, when the blood cannot clot, bleeding from minor or minimal trauma can occur, and even bleeding without injury or trauma may occur. This can include bruises, bleeding from the mouth or gastrointestinal tract, bleeding from cuts or circumcision.

Bleeding can occur anywhere in the body, including in the brain, which can be catastrophic.

VKDB can occur from birth and through several months of life. Bleeding in the brain from VKDB, one of the most serious consequences, can occur at any time from birth to up to 6 months or so and can occur unexpectedly and suddenly. Vitamin K given at birth can prevent this risk of bleeding.

Recent findings suggest that tse: Vitamin K is a necessary vitamin that all humans need. Vitamin K is not a vaccination.

Newborns need vitamin K to prevent serious, significant, and often catastrophic bleeding during their first several months of life.

Vitamin K has been given to newborns in the United States for close to 70 years, is safe, is studied, and is proven to help prevent vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

I urge newly introduced parents to allow their newborns to receive the vitamin K injection at birth — it protects them, keeps them healthy, is proven safe, and is recommended.

#166930. Industry News: Phenomenological Bioethics: What Does It Mean to Die Well?

Industry News: Phenomenological Bioethics: What Does It Mean to Die Well?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the modern fast-paced world, many of us spend little time consciously thinking about our inevitable deaths until we are directly confronted by them.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to historian Philippe Ariès, death was once a communal and intimate event within the Western world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Co-authored by Mark Shelvock and Daniel Wyzynski.

Recent findings suggest that in the modern fast-paced world, many of us spend little time consciously thinking about our inevitable deaths until we are directly confronted by them. This existential confrontation can occur through a upcoming diagnosis, a loved one’s health declining, an unexpected tragedy, or perhaps when we put on our favourite hospital drama on TV.

Recent findings suggest that according to historian Philippe Ariès, death was once a communal and intimate event within the Western world. People died at home, surrounded by family, within a web of cultural and/or religious rituals.1 Over the course of the 20th century, however, dying became more medicalized; relocated from the home into hospitals and institutions, and transferred from the hands of families into the hands of healthcare providers. As medical interventions progressed and the ability to keep death at bay grew, the location of care shifted to a place where more invasive interventions could be performed — and now a common request that arises in the hospital is for the medical staff to "do everything" to prevent death.

In North America, and across much of the Western world, many people today have little personal experience with dying or death. Alternatively, movies and TV may have taught them to expect a tranquil death that rarely matches reality. This cultural estrangement has real consequences for individuals, families, healthcare providers, and the health system.

One of the most vital distinctions in end-of-life care is between disease and illness. Disease is objective; the measurable, diagnosable change in the body that a clinician can identify and treat. Illness, on the other hand, is subjective and deeply personal. Illness is the lived experience of being unwell, which may include experiences of fear, fatigue, grief, and a loss of identity or other personal struggles that no medical chart can fully capture.

Modern medicine has become extraordinarily good at treating disease, but far less attentive to illness, and to dying.1,2,3 Yet for the person who has become a “patient”, illness is what often matters the most: what it means, how it feels, and what it does to a person's sense of self, their life story, and the impact it has on the people they love the most.4.

Pain follows the same logic. Many clinicians learn early that pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, and two people with identical diagnoses can suffer in radically different ways. Dying, then, is never simply a medical event. It is a disorienting, multidimensional, and existentially raw time in a person’s life.

The physician-author Atul Gawande put the problem plainly: people facing serious illness have priorities beyond simply prolonging their lives.2 They want to avoid suffering, remain psychologically present, feel connected to the people they love, and they want to reflect on the sense that their lives have been complete and meaningful. The dominant model of technological medical care, Gawande argued, has frequently failed to meet these needs in the 21st century.

What people need at the end of life is not always more intervention, but more presence, listening, psychosocial supports, and more honest conversations about what really matters. This is where phenomenological bioethics enters; it is not just abstract theory, but a practical human philosophy and orientation towards authentic care.

It has been revealed that phenomenology is the philosophical study of lived experience, and grapples with what it is like to be a conscious, embodied, mortal, and vulnerable human being. The philosopher Fredrik Svenaeus invites us to start with a unique person’s experience of suffering.

This approach asks clinicians and caregivers alike to sit with questions that no brain scan or blood panel can answer:.

Industry observers note that dying well is not about achieving some idealized exit, or being stoic, entirely peaceful, or free from all fear and suffering. It is about being seen as our own person, dying on our own terms: as a full human being with a history, a body, a web of relationships, and a particular way of making meaning in the world.

These questions are not morbid but generous, and asking them is one of the most profound acts of care available to us.

Sources indicate that we also acknowledge that phenomenological bioethics has significant limitations. It is difficult to scale its recommendations when faced with institutional and system-wide limitations; further, existentially informed approaches demand time, humility, and relational skills that constrained budgets and widespread burnout make hard to sustain. Still, it offers what medical treatments cannot supply on their own; a way of approaching dying as a fundamentally human experience, and not merely a set of clinical problems to be managed.

To our readers: the question worth asking now, not at the bedside or in crisis, but here, in the quiet of an ordinary day, is: What might it mean for you to die well, and can you talk about what dying well means to you and your loved ones?

According to recent reports, this article was co-authored with Daniel Wyzynski, a Clinical Ethicist, associate scientist, and adjunct research professor at Western University. Daniel specializes in clinical ethics, complex medical deliberation, mental health ethics, and patient-centred and family-centered care within acute and long-term care settings.

1. Ariès, P. (1981). The hour of our death. Knopf.

3. Svenaeus, F. (2017). Phenomenological bioethics: Medical technologies, human suffering, and the meaning of being alive. Routledge.

4. Frank, A. W. (1995). The wounded storyteller: Body, illness, and ethics. University of Chicago Press.

If you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative upcoming headphones and earbuds have been announced, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

Sources indicate that first up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the upcoming Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

According to recent reports, the 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously revealed $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

It has been revealed that compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned firm expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

In a recent development, being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

As for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

Industry observers note that the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

In a recent development, to ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

  • For this project, Electrogenic carefully removed the internal combustion-based engine, transmission, and fuel system from the City of London Corporation’s official ’73 Phantom VI limo and replaced it with a 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motor putting out 310 Nm (~230 lb-ft) of torque.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you wake up tomorrow as the esteemed Lord Mayor of London, you’ll want to make a properly dignified entrance. To make sure your arrival turns the right heads, Electrogenic has taken the Mayor’s 1973 Roll-Royce Phantom VI and turned it into a properly traditional standard-bearer with modern electric power.

The stately, stylish, and silent electric Rolls-Royce car made its public debut at last month’s Salon Privé weekend at Blenheim Palace, where it joined a growing fleet of classic Rollers that have received Elctrogenic’s electric conversion, including the stunning Mulliner-bodied 1929 Phantom II that we covered back in 2023.

For this project, Electrogenic carefully removed the internal combustion-based engine, transmission, and fuel system from the City of London Corporation’s official ’73 Phantom VI limo and replaced it with a 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motor putting out 310 Nm (~230 lb-ft) of torque. Sharp-eyed readers will note those numbers are significantly lower than what you’d expect from the 6.2L L410 V8 fitted with twin SU carburetors (as it was in the standard ’73 IV), but since those numbers were never officially published, we would say that the power available from the upcoming electric drivetrain is similarly adequate for Mayoral use.

Power for the electric motor comes from a 62 kWh li-ion battery fitted under the hood bonnet, and offers more than enough range to get the Lord Mayor to their appointments in and around the city.

To ensure the heads of the heads of the city don’t bob in an undignified manner while on parade, Electrogenic added a “ceremonial” drive mode that trims power and torque and softens the throttle map, so the chauffeur can more easily hold the crawling pace demanded by civic processions and state occasions.

Sources indicate that “We were honored to be asked to electrify this significant motor car, and to play a part in the City of London Corporation’s journey to net zero,” states Steve Drummond, chief executive of Electrogenic. “When it was rolled out in the late 1960s, the Rolls-Royce VI was the most refined and dignified limousine on the road. Now, thanks to electrification, its core character has been enhanced further: it is whisper quiet, effortless to drive with swift performance, and emits zero tailpipe emissions.”.

It's notable for government to be seen to follow it's own policy.

A standard complaint by oil lobbyists is that government vehicles aren't electrified.

Only 374 Phantom VIs were built between 1968 and 1990, with this 3 meter-long coach-built limousine having been commissioned during the mayoralty of Alderwoman Dame Susan Langley DBE, the 697th Lord Mayor of the City of London. The Phantom was converted as part of the Corporation’s broader effort to achieve a net zero carbon emissions goal from its own operations in 2027.

FDA Initiates Labeling Changes for GLP-1s Due to Rare But Serious Eye Disease Risk

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) unveiled on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S.
  • A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 users have a new symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.

Industry observers note that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) unveiled on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S. labels for Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity, Mounjaro, and Zepbound already warn about diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye disease, according to each drug’s prescribing information.The two conditions affect different parts of the eye. Diabetic retinopathy damages tiny blood vessels in the retina, the layer at the back of the eye that senses light, according to the National Eye Institute. NAION damages the optic nerve when it doesn’t get enough blood, according to the FDA’s announcement.Mihail Zilbermint, MD, director of endocrine hospitalists at Johns Hopkins, told Healthline he hasn’t seen NAION in his patients. He has seen vision worsen in some people after they start a GLP-1.“But we believe that’s probably related to rapid improvement in their sugar control, which can also be seen in someone who is starting insulin,” Zilbermint said.

A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.

Recent findings suggest that the study found a higher risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, than in people prescribed other diabetes or weight-loss drugs.The authors wrote that more research is needed to determine whether semaglutide causes NAION.Joseph F. Rizzo III, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, served as the study’s corresponding author.

In a 2024 podcast, Rizzo said he and a resident saw three patients with NAION who were taking semaglutide for about a week.“And because NAION is a fairly uncommon disorder in the general population, the fact that we had three within a relatively short period of time led me to suspect that there was a higher risk of developing NAION in patients on semaglutide,” Rizzo said. The FDA analyzed clinical trials for multiple GLP-1 drugs and noted that NAION cases were reported with every GLP-1 on the market, according to its announcement. Those findings led the FDA to require the warning for the entire drug class, the agency told Healthline.

According to recent reports, about 70% to 80% of people with NAION first notice vision loss when they wake up, according to StatPearls. The FDA listed these symptoms:.

No treatment has been proven to reverse vision loss from NAION, according to StatPearls.

“Patients experiencing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye should contact their healthcare professional immediately and should not stop their medication without consulting their provider first,” the FDA told Healthline.

In the announcement, the agency told doctors to promptly refer patients with suspected NAION to an ophthalmologist.

The FDA listed these possible risk factors for NAION:.

The FDA told Healthline that many people who take GLP-1s also have these conditions, which made reports of NAION in GLP-1 consumers “challenging” to interpret.

Across 126 clinical trials, the FDA found about 6 NAION cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for a year, and about 4 per 100,000 people taking a placebo or another diabetes drug for a year.In real-world data, NAION was more common with GLP-1s than with one type of diabetes pill, but the FDA found no significant increase compared with another type, the agency told Healthline.Zilbermint stated patients who saw the news have worried about losing their vision. He tells them that “many of the serious harms, including the potential harm of NAION, are rare.”“The overall risk is still very small,” he said.

Regulators in other countries have added NAION warnings, mostly for semaglutide:.

The FDA told Healthline the benefits of GLP-1s “continue to outweigh their risks when used as directed.”The FDA has also approved some GLP-1s to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, and treat sleep apnea and a type of liver disease.Zilbermint mentioned that “for most of my patients with obesity, diabetes and heart disease, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.”“But we definitely have to decide patient by patient,” he added.

The labeling change applies to these medications, according to the FDA’s announcement:.

As of publication, the FDA’s online label database did not yet show the new warning on the drugs’ labels.

Rare rhino birth caught on camera at England’s Chester Zoo

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England.
  • The sex and weight have not been declared yet, and the calf also does not have a name.
  • Sources indicate that at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage reveals rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been declared yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

Sources indicate that at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

It has been revealed that the team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she showed signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos remarked in an e-mailed statement. “It was a massive moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”.

Industry observers note that both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

It has been revealed that “Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”.

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

Industry observers note that while the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species currently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This upcoming calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

“Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”.

BYD’s luxury SUV pulled a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet on just two wheels [Video]

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, most SUVs are lucky to tow a small trailer without breaking a sweat.
  • The Bao 5 made its European debut at the Goodwood Festival of Speed (FOS) in July, the first SUV from BYD’s “premium technology-focused” brand, Denza.
  • As Denza’s first SUV designed specifically for Europe, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, said the company is “confident that the Bao 5 will be a huge hit,” offering the perfect mix of off-road ability, luxury, and advanced technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most SUVs are lucky to tow a small trailer without breaking a sweat. BYD’s newly introduced luxury SUV had a slightly bigger challenge: pulling a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet. And somehow, it did it on just two wheels. The video is worth a look.

The Bao 5 made its European debut at the Goodwood Festival of Speed (FOS) in July, the first SUV from BYD’s “premium technology-focused” brand, Denza.

As Denza’s first SUV designed specifically for Europe, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, said the company is “confident that the Bao 5 will be a huge hit,” offering the perfect mix of off-road ability, luxury, and advanced technology.

The SUV uses BYD’s DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) plug-in hybrid powertrain, which BYD noted is the “world’s first off-road-dedicated hybrid architecture/”.

BYD’s off-road PHEV powertrain features three electric motors (one on each axle and a third generator) and a 1.5L turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 536 horsepower (544 PS) and 560 lb-ft (760 Nm) of torque.

BYD boasted that “Those figures – well clear of PHEV rivals’ and comfortably more than conventional diesel SUVs’ – are enough for a 0-100km/h time of just 4.8 seconds.”.

To top it off, BYD added a double wishbone front and rear suspension with its DiSus-P intelligent body system, plus front and rear intelligent electronic differential locks with millisecond-level response to improve traction and performance.

The Bao 5 is equipped with a 31.8 kWh BYD Blade Battery that delivers a pure-electric WLTP range of up to 56 miles (90 km). And on a full tank and a full charge, the WLTP combined range is 537 miles (835 km).

To prove the upcoming luxury SUV’s capabilities, BYD put it to the ultimate test — towing a Boeing 747 jumbo jet using just two wheels.

While pulling a 180-tonne, or nearly 400,000-pound, jumbo jet on four wheels is impressive in itself, Denza’s engineers wanted to push it further, doing something never tried before to showcase its off-road DMO technology.

Industry observers note that the Bao 5 was put to the test at Dunsfold Aerodrome airfield in Surrey, England. It successfully pulled the jumbo jet in each of its three runs: one on four wheels, one on three, and the last on just two wheels.

Combined, the SUV towed the 747 for a total of 1,600 meters, or close to a mile, which BYD said is about four laps around a standard-size athletic track.

Industry observers note that while a feat like this sounds impressive on paper, keep in mind that planes are designed to roll with as little resistance as possible. Top Gear pulled a 747 with a Touareg a while back. The main thing a pushback rig has is weight so that it can maintain traction. That's why BYD put nearly 10,000 lbs of ballast in the back - so it wouldn't spin its wheels on the tarmac.

It's still interesting, to be sure, especially removing two wheels.

BYD remarked the Bao 5 was a standard, production-spec Ultimate trim model, and the modifications were minimal.

According to recent reports, A towing attachment was added, while the interior passenger seats were removed to make space for the 9,920 lb (4,500 kg) of ballast for the two-wheel pull test. In addition, Denza added small stabilizers to each axle so the vehicle remained balanced on two wheels.

After each run, the vehicle was inspected and confirmed to show no signs of stress on the powertrain, chassis, or tires.

The Bao 5 SUV normally has a towing capacity of over 5,500 lbs (2,500 kg), according to BYD’s Denza brand.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.
  • According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.
  • However, upcoming research published in the November 2026 issue of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.

According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.

However, upcoming research published in the November 2026 issue of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.

In fact, having a history of reacting to peanuts and positive allergy testing on their own may not be sufficient to diagnose a peanut allergy for many infants.

The study’s authors suggest that a threshold oral food challenge — in which the child is given increasing amounts of the suspected food allergen under medical supervision to look for an allergic reaction — should be routinely considered to help confirm peanut allergy.

This additional testing could safely prevent children who are not allergic to peanuts from undergoing unnecessary treatment with oral immunotherapy.

It could also spare families from burdensome food restrictions and allergy precautions.

The researchers’ goal was to evaluate the accuracy and safety of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Path to Tolerance (ADAPT) peanut oral immunotherapy program, which was established in 2024 at 10 public children’s hospitals across Australia.

This program provides a standardized approach to evaluating and treating infants with suspected peanut allergies.

The study included infants who had experienced a mild to moderate reaction to peanut before 12 months of age and had evidence of peanut sensitization through allergy testing.

Researchers reviewed medical records to examine how accurately the program’s approach identified peanut allergies and whether it could safely guide treatment.

A key part of the evaluation was a threshold oral food challenge. The challenge involved up to seven doses, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams of peanut protein.

Medical teams monitored the infants for reactions and provided treatment when necessary.

It has been revealed that researchers reviewed records from April 2024 through October 2025. During that period, 1,275 infants were assessed through the program, and 778 underwent an oral food challenge.

The researchers also examined allergy test results and whether infants who reacted during the challenges could begin oral immunotherapy at an appropriate starting dose.

At the time of the oral food challenge, the infants had a median age of 13 months.

Of the 778 infants who underwent an oral food challenge, 507 (65.2%) had an allergic reaction.

However, 271 (34.8%) did not react to peanut during the supervised test, despite having a history of a previous reaction and positive allergy test results.

These findings suggest that relying on medical history and allergy tests alone may lead some infants to be labeled with a peanut allergy when they can actually tolerate the food.

According to recent reports, among the infants who reacted during the challenges, 61 experienced anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. This represented 12% of infants with a positive challenge and 7.8% of all infants who underwent testing. Medical teams safely managed these severe allergic reactions.

Researchers also found that infants who reacted to peanut generally had higher skin prick test results and Ara h 2-specific IgE levels than those who did not react.

However, these test results did not reliably indicate how much peanut would trigger a reaction or how severe that reaction would be.

Of the 394 infants who began peanut oral immunotherapy, 384 (97.5%) successfully started treatment at a dose below the amount that had triggered a reaction during their food challenge.

The researchers say these findings support considering supervised oral food challenges to confirm suspected peanut allergies before starting treatment or recommending long-term avoidance.

Erin Banta, MD, a board certified allergist and immunologist who treats both children and adults at Latitude Food Allergy Care in Great Neck, New York, remarked these findings are significant because they provide evidence for early use of oral food challenges in infants with peanut reactions.

“In those with mild-moderate prior reactions to peanut, early oral food challenge may allow for either delabeling of food allergy (in 1/3 of the patients in this study) or diagnosis of food allergy,” she told Healthline.

Banta, who wasn’t involved in the study, added that early delabeling takes a significant burden off the patient and their family.

“On the other hand,” she explained, “early diagnosis allows for early initiation of treatment with oral immunotherapy at a time in the patient’s life associated with the greatest success rates.”.

Banta further noted that the study offers different pathways for oral immunotherapy based on the patient’s reaction threshold. This means that some patients may be able to complete treatment more promptly due to their individual threshold dose.

Lindsey Forstie, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with clinical training and experience in allergy and asthma care at Carefree Allergy in Phoenix, AZ, added that while further evaluation may be needed to confirm a peanut allergy diagnosis, it’s vital for parents not to try introducing peanuts at home.

“Instead, they should speak with their pediatrician or allergist about appropriate testing and whether a supervised food challenge is safe and necessary,” she remarked.

According to Forstie, who was also not part of the study, the goal is to avoid unnecessary food restrictions while also keeping children safe.

According to recent reports, “The key message is that not every positive allergy test means a child has a food allergy,” she told Healthline. “Accurate diagnosis helps protect children while allowing those who are not allergic to enjoy a more normal, less restrictive diet.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As no-drip, low-noise job sites become more the global rule rather than the exception, Volvo’s incredibly versatile EWR150 Electric wheeled excavators are proving to be a smart addition to construction and municipal fleets – that’s proving true in Luxembourg, as well.

Industry observers note that the Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator is helping the postage stamp nation of Luxembourg connect natural freshwater springs to a planned water reservoir, but the work has to be done in an existing groundwater protection zone, where even the smallest fuel spills or oil leaks could have serious consequences. An ideal opportunity, in other words, for a battery electric machine like the EWR150 Electric to shine.

“Sometimes I miss the sound of the engine,” states Thomas Weber, an operator on the project who’d previously worked with the conventional EWR150 wheeled excavator. “But the quieter operation of the EWR150 Electric is more beneficial for me, personally. Compared to the diesel equivalent, I find the performance and power to be identical.”.

Volvo CE took to LinkedIn to share the work being done by the Luxemburgers at construction firm Elenz, touting the Volvo’s clean, quiet running in this highly environment.

For their part, Elenz executives are equally excited about the latest machine. “Going electric is not a regulation, but a requirement for this particular job,” explains Christoph Schommer, Managing Director of Elenz. “We are thoroughly impressed by the EWR150 Electric. Its low noise level is a major advantage here. At the same time, the machine offers plenty of power and consistently delivers the same level of energy.”.

It has been revealed that the EWR150 Electric is built around a 270 kWh, 600V li-ion battery pack powering an electric drive motor that’s backed by a KERS-style hydraulic boom energy-recovery system that works like regenerative braking to extend the machine’s operating time. A 0.67 m³ (~0.9 yd³) bucket with 108.5-kN (~ 24,390 lb.) breakout force is standard, and offers a, 8.95 meter (~29 foot) maximum digging reach and 5.23 meter (~17 foot) digging depth. Volvo indicates the machine can typically operate for 8–10 hours depending on the application.

It has been revealed that elenz is charging their EWR150 Electric overnight using a 32A L2 connection at a nearby sewage treatment plant, which also serves as the project office and a secure parking location for site equipment. By charging overnight, when Elenz’ crew isn’t working, the tech giant has been able to integrate the significant BEV without changing their existing work schedules.
